posture: The target file is unusually careful and its transcription work survives adversarial re-reading almost intact. I re-derived every wire list it claims to have image-verified, independently confirmed six of its eight binding rulings, image-verified two of its own stated open items and closed them in its favour, and found ZERO fabricated wires and ZERO hallucinated terminal letters. The file's tier C criterion reads 'Any program touching D0..D19, M+, M-, or the RUN/STOP/ARM jacks', and its tier C pass criterion is 'deferred. Do not attempt until the rotary timing model exists.' The file therefore simultaneously says build this first and do not attempt this.

refuted.note_on_the_right_fix: The defensible repair is to split tier C, not to move the program. II-EXP2 and I-EXP11 need only the STATIC dial-position-to-contact mapping (knob at n closes D16-Dn); neither runs the motor. Tier C as written conflates 'needs rotary contact geometry' with 'needs the motor stepping model'. Proposed: C1 = static rotary position, buildable now; C2 = motor stepping, deferred. That is a judgement call and must be labelled as one, not slipped in.

refuted.claim: II-EXP2's expected script, step 1, asserts then.lamps = {"4": "ON"}; step 2 asserts then.lamps = {"4": "OFF"}.
refuted.correction: Wrong observable class. The printed page says 'Relay light 4 comes ON to indicate that a four is being stored' and 'relay light 4 goes OFF'. A relay light is the indicator built into a relay section (terminals nC-nE); the BINARY OUTPUT lamps are terminals nA-nB and are a different observable in the file's own schema, which keeps separate 'lamps' and 'relays' maps. Decisive: II-EXP2's 23-wire program contains NO A or B terminal at all, so no binary-output lamp is even in the circuit. A fixture generated from this record would assert the state of an unwired lamp. The assertion must be relays = {"4": "ON"} / {"4": "OFF"}.
refuted.evidence: book2-3-4.pdf PDF p13 (printed p.7), pdftotext -layout, steps 1 and 2 verbatim; and the wire list above, which has no nA/nB terminal. refuted.claim: named_fallback FALLBACK-PWRUP-COLD, behaviour clause: 'A circuit that latches itself on during that first settle (the self-locking memory, for instance) is expected to come up ON - that is a real property of the circuit, not a violation of the fallback.'
refuted.correction: The named example is electrically backwards. II-SELFLOCK is 1+/1Y, 1+/1H, 1X/1C, 1-/1F, 1G/1A, 1B/1-, 1C/1A. The holding path is 1+ -> 1H (relay 1's contact common) -> 1G (relay 1's NORMALLY OPEN contact) -> 1A -> 1C -> relay lamp -> 1E -> coil -> 1F -> minus. At cold start relay 1 is unoperated, so 1H-1G is OPEN, the coil sees nothing, and the relay stays OFF. The self-locking memory comes up OFF and latches only after pushbutton 1 has been pressed once. The general fallback rule is sound; this worked example is not, and a fixture author following the sentence literally would write a wrong step-1 expectation for one of the file's own tier-B seed programs.
refuted.evidence: Wire list from verify-programs.json missed_programs_book_ii, II-SELFLOCK (printed p.10, PDF p16) [likely, OCR-sourced]. Contact polarity H=common, G=normally open, J=normally closed is [verified] and derivable two ways from primary text: (a) III-RELAYNOT, book2-3-4.pdf PDF p50, uses 1+/1H, 1J/2A so that lamp 2 is ON when relay 1 is OFF - J must be normally closed; (b) III-RELAYAND corrected by ER-12 uses 1+/1H, 1G/2H so that lamp 3 is ON only when BOTH relays are ON - G must be normally open.

refuted.claim: not_settled_by_the_sources item 1: 'Relay pull-in and drop-out times, and contact transfer order (break-before-make vs make-before-break). ... No manual gives a millisecond figure.'
refuted.correction: Contact transfer order IS settled for pushbuttons and for the rotary switch, in Book I, in body text, explicitly, and it is called out there as load-bearing. Only RELAY contact transfer order and the millisecond figures remain open. Bundling three separate questions into one 'not settled' item hides a fact the simulator needs.
refuted.evidence: book1.pdf printed p.9 (PDF p11), verbatim: 'One light always goes OFF before the other light comes ON. There is a position, with the pushbutton only partly depressed, where both lights are OFF. ... The switch breaks one connection before it makes the other connection. The pushbuttons are thus called "break-before-make" switches. This is important because it shows that the normally open contact is never connected directly to the normally closed contact, even for a very short time. This feature is necessary for the proper operation of some MINIVAC circuits.' And book1.pdf printed p.21 (PDF p23), verbatim: 'Notice that light 5 goes OFF before light 6 comes ON. This shows that the rotary switch is designed to disconnect the arm from one contact before making connection with the next contact. The switch operation is described as "break-before-make," and thus is similar to the pushbutton switches.' [verified from text layer - both are clean body text, not display headings]

downgraded.claim: 'SAME FLIP-FLOP TOPOLOGY, different indicator tap' / headline 'Book IV's second-version flip-flop is the SAME circuit relabelled - identical in five of six electrical nets - differing only in where indicator lamp 5's anode taps' / consequence 'they will agree in the stable states and may differ transiently.'
downgraded.downgrade_to: The net computation is correct and both wire lists are now verified, so the STRUCTURAL finding stands. The word 'only' and the stable-state prediction do not. On this machine an indicator lamp is a series element in the coil path, not a passive tap - the errata itself says so: ER-21, 'The circuit below by-passes the relay indicator lights so that full voltage is supplied to the relay coils, causing them to pull in more reliably.' Moving lamp 5's anode from the {5E,6G} node (the relay-lamp/coil junction, where in Book II it parallels relay 5's own indicator lamp) to the {5F,5H,6F} node (the coil's far end and contact common) changes coil loading, not just what a bulb displays. 'They will agree in the stable states' is an untagged inference with no primary support and should be tagged [unverified] or dropped.

[verified]
downgraded.keep: The file's operational conclusion - keep both as separate fixtures, do NOT unify the wire lists, assert lamp 5 in both - is right and should survive unchanged.

downgraded.claim: ER-ALTCOUNTER expected: 'Not printed on the errata sheet - it defers to Book IV printed p.72. The expected-state script must be lifted from IV-EXP1 and re-pointed at this wire list.'
downgraded.downgrade_to: This is presented as a mechanical operation. It is an inference, and a risky one. Book IV printed p.72 asserts its observables as 'Binary output lights 4, 5 and 6 will read OFF, OFF, ON or 001'. recovered_material.note: Transcribed here so the corpus builder does not have to re-open these pages. All from pdftotext -layout of book2-3-4.pdf unless marked as an image read.

IV-EXP1_program_printed_p72_pdf_p78.name: Experiment 1: A Three-Bit Binary Counter (Full program for Binary Counter)
IV-EXP1_program_printed_p72_pdf_p78.tag_reason: text layer only - I did not render this page. Two glyph risks remain: the plus signs (1G/1+, 3G/3+, 5G/5+, 6Y/6+) and the pair 1B/1- which OCR shows as 'IB/1—'. Needs one 300-dpi crop of PDF p78 to reach [verified].
printed_procedure_verbatim: 1. Turn power ON. Push pushbutton 6 and release. Binary output lights 4, 5 and 6 will read OFF, OFF, ON or 001. The Binary Counter is displaying a 1.
2. Push pushbutton 6 again and release. Binary output lights 4, 5 and 6 will now read OFF, ON, OFF or 010. The Binary Counter is now displaying a 2.

3. Push and release pushbutton 6 several times. Each time after releasing the pushbutton, note the binary number displayed in lights 4, 5 and 6. Compare your numbers with the table of binary numbers on page 66.
IV-EXP1_program_printed_p72_pdf_p78.printed_bit_assignment_verbatim: 'the low order flip-flop (represented by light 6) changes each time the pushbutton is pushed and released. The low order flip-flop represents 1's (units). The next flip-flop to the left (represented by light 5) changes every other time... And of course, the high order flip-flop (represented by light 4) changes every fourth time...'
IV-EXP1_program_printed_p72_pdf_p78.printed_wrap_verbatim: 'You will notice that the counter repeats after it has reached 7.'
IV-EXP1_program_printed_p72_pdf_p78.simulator_note: Light 4 = MSB (4's), light 5 = 2's, light 6 = LSB (1's). This is the observable mapping DG-02 says cannot be assumed to carry over to ER-ALTCOUNTER.

IV_binary_counter_sequence_chart_printed.what: BINARY COUNTER - SEQUENCE OF OPERATIONS. Printed as seven columns; the manual states 'the chart is read from right to left'. Rows are paired: for each count, an UP row and a DOWN row.
IV_binary_counter_sequence_chart_printed.tag_reason: pdftotext -layout only. Three cells in the Flip-Flop C column render as blank in the text layer (the UP rows for counts 2, 4 and 6). By the counter's own logic those cells must read 0, but I am NOT writing 0 into them - that would be inference presented as transcription. ONE 300-dpi crop of PDF p77 settles all three and promotes this whole table to [verified]. It is the single highest-value remaining image read in the program corpus.
IV_binary_counter_sequence_chart_printed.why_this_is_the_prize: Seventeen printed rows of ground truth for a sequential circuit, including the carry signals, and it costs one image read.

IV-FF2_printed_trace_image_verified.applies_to: IV-FF2 (SINGLE-INPUT FLIP-FLOP - SECOND VERSION), book2-3-4.pdf PDF p76, printed p.70
IV-FF2_printed_trace_image_verified.read_from: my own 300-dpi render of PDF p76
IV-FF2_printed_trace_image_verified.preamble_verbatim: 'We now have a single-input flip-flop with contacts free for a carry signal. With the power OFF, program this flip-flop on your MINIVAC 601. Then:'
steps_verbatim: 1. Turn power ON. Notice that both relays 5 and 6 are OFF.
2. Push and release pushbutton 6. Notice that both relays 5 and 6 are now ON.
3. Push pushbutton 6, but do not release. Notice that relay 5 is OFF; relay 6 is ON. We want a carry signal to occur NOW.

steps.source: printed p.70 step 3 ('but do not release')

IV-FF2_printed_trace_image_verified.note: Step 1 here is a PRINTED power-up assertion, so it does NOT need FALLBACK-PWRUP-COLD. It is also the strongest single piece of evidence FOR that fallback.

IV-FF2-CARRY_printed_p70.read_from: my own 300-dpi render of PDF p76
IV-FF2-CARRY_printed_p70.printed_addition_verbatim: 'To add the carry signal, we will add the connections: 5G/5N  6K/4A / 5L/6L  4B/4-'
IV-FF2-CARRY_printed_p70.printed_observable_verbatim: 'Light 4 will now indicate that a carry is taking place.'

contact_polarity_settled.pushbuttons: Y = common (arm), X = normally open (closes when pressed), Z = normally closed (opens when pressed). [verified] book1.pdf printed p.9: 'The normally closed contact (Y/Z) may be used to complete a circuit when the pushbutton is UP, and the normally open contact (X/Y) may be used to complete a circuit when the pushbutton is DOWN.'
contact_polarity_settled.relay_first_contact_set: H = common, G = normally open, J = normally closed. [verified] by two independent circuits: III-RELAYNOT (1+/1H, 1J/2A - lamp 2 ON while relay 1 is OFF) and III-RELAYAND as corrected by ER-12 (1+/1H, 1G/2H - lamp 3 ON only when both relays are ON).
contact_polarity_settled.relay_second_contact_set: K, L, N. By analogy L = common, K and N the two contacts - NOT settled by anything I read. Book IV printed p.69 confirms only that the second set exists and that IV-FF1 consumes it ('since all contacts on both relays are used'). What would settle it: the Maintenance Manual, or a 300-dpi read of the IV-FF1 circuit diagram on PDF p75.
contact_polarity_settled.transfer_order: Pushbuttons and the rotary switch are BREAK-BEFORE-MAKE, printed and emphasised. [verified] - see RF-05. Relay contact transfer order is genuinely not settled by anything I read.

fallback_judgement.fallback: FALLBACK-PWRUP-COLD - at power ON every relay coil is de-energised and every relay sits in its unoperated position; slide switches and dial hold their initial_settings; then iterate to fixpoint and only then assert step 1.
fallback_judgement.is_it_defensible: YES. It is physically correct for single-coil spring-return relays, which is what this machine has, and it is the only power-up rule any of these manuals asserts. It makes every fixture reproducible, and the alternative - modelling a power-up race - would be an invented model, which is the worse failure for this project.
fallback_judgement.is_it_honestly_labelled: YES, and better than most. It lives in a block called named_fallback, not among the findings. It carries an explicit what_would_overturn_it. It mandates that every assertion generated under it carry tag='unverified' and source='FALLBACK-PWRUP-COLD', and that the harness be able to list on demand which expectations rest on it rather than on print. That is the right shape for a fallback and it is not dressed up as a finding anywhere in the file.
fallback_judgement.additional_support_i_found: Book IV printed p.70 step 1, image-verified by me: 'Turn power ON. Notice that both relays 5 and 6 are OFF.' This is the fallback asserted in print for a BISTABLE circuit, which is the hard case, and it is the strongest single piece of evidence for the rule. Also Book I printed p.9 step 6: 'Turn the power switch ON. Light 2 comes on as soon as power is turned ON' - a cold-start-then-settle through a normally-closed contact.
fallback_judgement.its_one_defect: The worked example inside the behaviour clause is wrong - see RF-04. The self-locking memory comes up OFF, not ON, because its holding path runs through its own normally-open contact. Replace the example or delete it; the rule itself is unaffected.
fallback_judgement.verdict: Keep the fallback. Fix the example. Keep the tagging discipline exactly as written.

verdict: The transcription work in this file is sound - I re-derived twelve wire lists against the primary sources and found zero fabricated wires and zero invented terminal letters, and I closed two of its own stated open items (IV-FF2's wire list, the four Book VI errata notes) in its favour with fresh 300-dpi reads. Its failures are in framing and in tiering, not in reading: two tier-A assignments contradict its own tier-C rule, one expected value is recorded against the wrong observable class, one worked example inside the named fallback is electrically backwards, one 'not settled' item is settled in Book I, and it misses the richest printed expected-output table in the manual set. Trust its transcriptions; audit its tiers, its tags and its worked examples before generating a single fixture; and do not treat the gap as closed, because the corpus file it specifies does not exist.
